facts.topic: Camp regulation - who may hold camps

facts.note: Also covered by Bar & Bench: https://www.barandbench.com/view-point/meity-notifies-final-digital-personal-data-protection-rules-2025. Commentators cite the gazette references as G.S.R. 846(E) for the Rules and G.S.R. 843(E) for commencement; these were not read directly.

facts.claim: The phases are: from 13 Nov 2025, the Data Protection Board provisions; from 13 Nov 2026, the Consent Manager framework; from 13 May 2027, the remaining substantive obligations on data fiduciaries (notice, consent, security safeguards, breach reporting and others).
facts.source_title: DPDP Act 2023 and Rules 2025: Phased Implementation Timeline (Sansa Legal)
facts.note: One source gives 14 Nov 2026 and 14 May 2027, so the exact day should be checked against the gazette. Sources also disagree on which rule numbers took effect on day one.

facts.claim: MeitY consulted stakeholders on 23 January 2026 about shortening the compliance window from 18 to 12 months, which would make 13 November 2026 the core deadline. As of the latest sources (6 September 2026), this had not been notified, so 13 May 2027 remains the operative deadline.
facts.source_title: MeitY plans to cut short DPDP Compliance Timeline (Chambers)
facts.note: Whether anything was notified between 6 Sep and 11 Oct 2026 is not confirmed.

facts.claim: Section 7(i) of the DPDP Act lets employers process personal data without consent 'for the purposes of employment' or to safeguard the employer from loss or liability. The statutory examples are defensive, such as preventing corporate espionage and protecting trade secrets. Commentators disagree on how far it reaches, and its application to employee medical or health-test data is untested.
facts.source_title: Navigating Legitimate Use Exemption for Employee Data under DPDP Act 2023 (Bar & Bench)
facts.note: No source confirmed that health check-up results fall under 7(i). For the pitch, the safe position is to get explicit consent from each employee for the check-up and for any report shared with the employer.

facts.claim: Under the DPDP Act, consent must be for a specified purpose and limited to the personal data necessary for that purpose. Data principals must know what they are consenting to.
facts.source_title: DPDP Act: Balancing Employee Data & Privacy Rights (Mondaq / PSA Legal)
facts.note: Implication for the deck: Dhruv Diagnostics should collect consent from the employee, give individual results to the employee, and share only aggregated or anonymised data with the employer unless the employee consents. This is a recommendation, not a quoted rule.

facts.claim: Commentary raises the open question of whether employers must still get written consent for data classed as sensitive personal data under the older IT Act SPDI Rules (which include medical records) where DPDP legitimate use also applies. No answer was found.
facts.source_title: From Consent to Compliance: Implications of DPDP Act on Employment Practices (Bar & Bench)
facts.note: Unresolved in the sources found.

facts.note: The same list appears in a Lok Sabha answer: https://eparlib.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/958172/1/AU2315.pdf. The mca.gov.in text was not retrieved.

facts.claim: Rule 2(1)(d) of the Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014, as amended in 2021, excludes from CSR any activity that benefits the company's employees as defined in section 2(k) of the Code on Wages, 2019. Commentators read this as meaning activities exclusively for employees and their families do not qualify as CSR.
facts.source_title: Ushering a new CSR Regime (Khaitan & Co)
facts.note: Also covered by iPleaders: https://blog.ipleaders.in/analysis-new-csr-regime/ and NGO Experts: https://ngoexperts.com/blogs/csr-expenditure-rules. facts.claim: No official MCA statement was found saying blood donation camps are eligible CSR. Treating a community blood donation drive as 'preventive health care' under Schedule VII item (i) is a reasonable reading but is NOT confirmed. A drive limited to employees would likely fall under the employee-benefit exclusion.
facts.source_title: Looking beyond strict lines: CSR amidst pandemic (iPleaders)
facts.note: iPleaders reports that MCA circulars treat enabling access to, or better delivery of, public health systems as preventive health care. Check against the MCA CSR FAQs before claiming CSR eligibility in the deck.

facts.claim: Deloitte's 2022 report 'Mental health and well-being in the workplace' estimates that poor employee mental health costs Indian employers about US$14 billion (about Rs 1.1 lakh crore) a year. The breakdown is roughly Rs 14,000 crore from absenteeism, Rs 51,000 crore from presenteeism and Rs 45,000 crore from attrition.
facts.value: ~US$14 bn/yr; presenteeism is the largest component
facts.source_title: 'Unhealthy cost': Poor employee mental health costs India Inc around $14 billion yearly (People Matters)
facts.note: The Deloitte press release was returned as https://www2.deloitte.com/in/en/pages/life-sciences-and-healthcare/articles/mental-health-press-release-2022.html (the search result had a stray trailing backslash). These are modelled estimates from a survey of 3,995 employees, released 8 Sep 2022. They measure the cost of poor mental health, NOT the ROI of wellness programmes or check-ups.

facts.claim: In the Deloitte survey, about 80% of Indian respondents reported mental health issues in the past year, and 47% named workplace stress as the top factor. When their mental health was poor, 33% kept working, 29% took time off and 20% resigned.
facts.source_title: People Matters (reporting Deloitte 2022)

facts.claim: INDIA-WORKS (INtegrating DIAbetes prevention in WORKplaceS) is a peer-reviewed worksite diabetes-prevention programme in India. It ran at 11 worksites in 5 states (Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha), aimed at about 2,000 adults with prediabetes or unmedicated diabetes, used peer educators and text messages, and had HbA1c as its primary outcome. The 2023 paper in Implementation Science Communications reports how the programme was adapted and implemented, not whether it reduced HbA1c.
facts.source_title: Adapting and scaling a proven diabetes prevention program across 11 worksites in India: the INDIA-WORKS trial (PMC)
facts.note: Emory's study page (https://diabetes.emory.edu/research/worksite.html) describes eight worksites, which differs from the 11 in the paper. No published primary-effectiveness results (HbA1c, diabetes incidence) were found, so the deck should not claim it worked. It is fair to say Indian employers and researchers are testing workplace diabetes prevention.

facts.claim: No credible peer-reviewed Indian study was found that quantifies reduced absenteeism or higher productivity from workplace wellness or health check-up programmes. RAND and other international evidence was not searched because the search budget ran out.
facts.source_title: INDIA-WORKS implementation paper (closest Indian peer-reviewed workplace evidence found)
facts.note: Avoid ROI or absenteeism-reduction claims in the deck unless a source is added.

research.gaps:
All 18 WebSearch calls were used. WebFetch was unavailable, so no primary text was read directly: no gazette, no Lancet appendix, no MCA page. Every fact comes from search-result summaries of secondary or official-news pages.

Open items:
(a) Maharashtra-specific ICMR-INDIAB 2023 figures were not found. Only Phase I (2008-10) state figures are available.
(b) Official NFHS-5 Maharashtra decimals for anaemia were not checked against the fact sheet. The 54% (women) and 22% (men) figures come from a secondary summary.
(c) The exact scope of the OSH Central Rules 2026 Rule 5 is contested. As quoted, it covers dock work and building/construction work for employees aged 40 and over. Whether mines are included and whether factories were dropped differs between sources. Final Maharashtra OSH Rules are not confirmed as notified by 11 Oct 2026; the draft extends the 40+ check-up to every establishment. It was also not confirmed which government (Centre or State) is the appropriate government for typical Nagpur private employers.
(d) It was not confirmed whether MeitY's proposed 12-month DPDP acceleration was notified after 6 Sep 2026.
(e) The application of DPDP s.7(i) to employee health-test data is untested.
(f) CSR eligibility of blood donation camps was not confirmed by any MCA document, and the MCA CSR FAQ and Rules text were not retrieved.
(g) No Indian peer-reviewed evidence was found on absenteeism or productivity gains from wellness programmes. RAND and other international studies were not searched. The INDIA-WORKS effectiveness results were not found.

Recommended deck wording: say 'mandatory free annual check-ups for workers 40+ in notified sectors (dock, construction), and proposed for all establishments under Maharashtra's draft rules' rather than 'mandatory for all employees over 40'.

checks.reason: The PIB document is dated 11 Dec 2025 (file doc20251211...) and titled 'Labour Codes Upgrade Safety for Hazardous Sector Workers'. It lists a free annual health check-up for all hazardous-sector workers, with no age threshold, plus pre-employment, periodic and post-exposure exams.

checks.claim: Government messaging said the labour codes would ensure free annual health check-ups for workers above 40.
checks.reason: Confirmed, with an important new detail for the pitch. On 7 May 2026 Labour Minister Mansukh Mandaviya launched a nationwide free annual health check-up initiative for workers aged 40+ under the Labour Codes, run through ESIC hospitals (launched at ESIC Basaidarapur, Delhi and 11 other ESIC hospitals). Treatment and medicines are provided through ESIC. ESIC-covered workers can therefore get a government-provided free check-up. The deck should present Dhruv Diagnostics as a convenient on-site or comprehensive option for employers, not as the only way to comply.

checks.claim: OSH (Central) Rules, 2026 notified 8 May 2026 as G.S.R. 345(E).
checks.reason: StaffNews reproduces the notification title 'G.S.R. 345(E) dated 08.05.2026', and Sansa Legal and other trackers agree.

checks.claim: Rule 5 of the OSH Central Rules: free annual medical examination for employees aged 40+ in dock work and building/other construction work, by a qualified medical practitioner, with a Form VIII certificate.
checks.reason: Shiftelio and Taxheal both quote the rule 5 text as limited to dock and building/construction work. One search summary also said employers may use ESIC facilities, but I could not tie that to a specific source, so treat it as unverified. The deck must not say 'mandatory for all employees over 40' under central law.

checks.reason: The dispute persists. Shiftelio says mines fall under rule 109 and factories were dropped from the final rule 5, while Lexology and Legal500 summaries list mines alongside dock and construction. The gazette text was not readable through search, so this cannot be resolved.

checks.claim: Maharashtra has only draft OSH rules (Draft Maharashtra OSH and Working Conditions (Labour) Rules, 2026), which would extend the free annual check-up for 40+ employees to every establishment. Final rules not notified.
checks.reason: The draft status is confirmed: TeamLease dates the draft 30 April 2026, and TMS Services, updated early September 2026, says final rules were not yet notified and expects them around August-November 2026. Whether final rules were notified between early September and 11 October 2026 could not be confirmed. The deck should say 'proposed under Maharashtra's draft rules', not 'mandatory in Maharashtra'.

checks.claim: DPDP phased dates: Consent Manager framework from 13 Nov 2026; remaining obligations from 13 May 2027.
checks.reason: MirvoLegal (as at September 2026) states that Rule 4 commences one year after publication (13 Nov 2026), and that Rules 3, 5-16, 22 and 23 commence 18 months after publication (13 May 2027). This implies publication on 13 Nov 2025, consistent with the Rules being notified that day.

checks.claim: MeitY's proposal to shorten the DPDP compliance window from 18 to 12 months had not been notified; 13 May 2027 remains operative.
checks.reason: This now holds later than the researcher's 6 Sep date. MirvoLegal (as at 20 Sep 2026) found no amending notification, and a status update dated 28 Sep 2026 also found none. Nothing between 28 Sep and 11 Oct 2026 was checked.

checks.claim: CSR Rules (2021 amendment) rule 2(1)(d) exclude activities benefiting the company's employees as defined in s.2(k) of the Code on Wages, 2019.
checks.reason: Taxguru and Vinod Kothari confirm that this is one of six exclusions in the rule 2(1)(d) CSR definition. Vinod Kothari's FAQ reads it as excluding programmes aimed solely at employees; community programmes where employees have no special status are not automatically excluded. Employee-only check-ups are therefore not CSR, while public community health or blood donation camps may be, subject to MCA guidance (not confirmed).

research.gaps: I used all 18 searches; WebFetch was unavailable, so every figure comes from search-result summaries, not from reading the pages. Not found: (1) Published corporate rate cards, volume-discount tiers, minimum headcount for onsite camps, or whether onsite collection is free for corporate camps, from Dr Lal, Metropolis, Thyrocare, Redcliffe, Healthians, Apollo or Tata 1mg. Every source says to ask for a quote. (2) Any Nagpur-specific mammography price; only the national HCG range (Rs 1,600-12,700) was found. (3) A standalone TSH price in Nagpur; only a thyroid profile (Rs 500 at Max, page unclear) and a Rs 399 bundle that includes HbA1c and TSH. (4) Vitamin D, CBC and lipid single prices in Nagpur came only from Max, and the exact page is unclear. (5) Apollo 24|7 corporate package inclusions; prices only. (6) Explicit per-dependant or family add-on prices; only 1+1 bundle offers (Dr Lal Family 1+1, Redcliffe One Plus One in Nagpur) without prices. (7) Inclusions for Wockhardt Nagpur's executive packages. (8) The rule requiring free annual check-ups for workers 40+ (Wikipedia) is not checked against the primary text. Most retail prices are aggregator listings (Bajaj Finserv Health, PharmEasy, 1mg, Max) with no update date, so treat them as indicative and confirm before putting them in the deck.

checks.claim: Organisations are now required to provide free annual health check-ups for all workers above age 40 (Wikipedia).
checks.corrected_value: The four labour codes took effect on 21 Nov 2025. Government (PIB) material says employers must give workers above 40 a free annual health check-up, and a PIB release of 7 May 2026 announces a nationwide annual check-up initiative, including an ESIC programme for insured persons above 40. However, a more careful reading of the OSH Central Rules 2026 says rule 5 applies to dock work and building/construction employers, with mines under rule 109. On that reading, IT, services, BFSI and general manufacturing are not yet clearly covered nationally, and state rules may differ. Suggested deck wording: 'India's new labour codes (in force since 21 Nov 2025) provide for free annual health check-ups for workers over 40 - we help you comply.' Avoid saying 'all employers must'.
checks.reason: The PIB sources support the headline. Two independent analyses say the operative central rule is limited to specific sectors. The scope is disputed and still evolving, so the blanket 'all workers' wording is overstated.
